title: Marvel’s ‘X-Men ’97’ Season 3 Teaser Debuts at New York Comic-Con
description: “X-Men ’97” is coming back. The animated Marvel series has been renewed for Season 3 on Disney+ and a first look at the new episodes has been reveal
body:
“X-Men ’97” is coming back. The animated Marvel series has been renewed for Season 3 on Disney+ and a first look at the new episodes has been revealed.

	While at New York Comic Con, head of Marvel television, animation, comics and franchise Brad Winderbaum revealed a clip from Season 3, which opened with someone writing “Where are the X-Men?” in graffiti. We learn that the city has reached chaos as police have blocked off the city and closed the border, meaning the mutants can’t get across to Professor X’s school and have no place to stay unless they have letters of transit.
	

	A young mutant starts to sneak across before she’s caught and deemed a threat. Just as she’s about to be captured, a team of mutants comes to rescue her. 


	“Are you the X-Men?” the girl asks them. “No, we’re the brotherhood,” they reply. 

	The clip also showed Storm and Professor X driving together and discussing the conflict they’re facing with the president of the U.S.. They exit the car and arrive at Gambit and Rogue’s wedding, where Deadpool and She-Hulk are among those in attendance. 

	Season 2 of “X-Men ’97” aired its finale on Aug. 12 after Season 1 debuted in 2024 and continued the story of the popular ’90s cartoon “X-Men: The Animated Series.” The Disney+ series revived the original series, which ran on Fox Kids from 1992-1997, and brought the animated X-Men to a new generation of fans after Disney acquired Fox.

	The X-Men found themselves scattered across time in Season 2, which featured the evil, time-traveling villain Apocalypse as their new antagonist. In a climactic episode set in ancient Egypt, Prof. Charles Xavier and his heroes are unable to stop Apocalypse from killing Magneto, their perennial nemesis but occasional ally. They also battle against the government-sanctioned team X-Factor, which includes Magneto’s daughter Polaris, and X-Force, the rogue team led by Cyclops and Jean Grey’s son Cable (who’s also traveled back in time from the future).
	

	After Season 1 broke fans’ hearts with the death of X-Men member Gambit, Season 2 resurrects the card-throwing hero as one of Apocalypse’s Horsemen. The undead hero initially turns agains the X-Men and serves Apocalypse, but Gambit’s lover Rogue is able to save him by harnessing the enormous power of a Celestial and offering to sacrifice herself. Rogue is successful and brings Gambit back to life, but in a twist, their X-Men pal Nightcrawler trades places with her and sacrifices himself to keep Rogue alive. The finale also revealed that the shape-shifting mutant Mystique killed X-Factor leader Valerie Cooper and assumed her identity, and Mystique’s non-mutant son Graydon Creed is elected president of the United States.

schema.headline: Marvel’s ‘X-Men ’97’ Season 3 Teaser Debuts at New York Comic-Con

title: ‘Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man’ Season 2 Sets Release Date
description:
The animated series “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” has set its Season 2 release date on Disney+.

	The second season will debut Jan. 13, 20
body:
The animated series “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” has set its Season 2 release date on Disney+.

	The second season will debut Jan. 13, 2027.

	Season 1 premiered in early 2025 and introduced a young, animated version of Spidey, voiced by Hudson Thames, who’s joined by some new and familiar faces in an alternate universe. The show takes place in a separate world from Tom Holland’s MCU character and follows the early days of Peter Parker’s web-slinging career. Instead of Tony Stark showing Peter the superhero ropes, “Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man” puts Norman Osborn, better known in the comics as the Green Goblin and who’s voiced by Colman Domingo, in a mentor role to Spidey. And instead of Mary Jane or Ned Leeds from the MCU, Peter is joined by his friends Nico Minoru, who has mystical sorcerer abilities, and Harry Osborne, the rich son of Norman.
	

	At the end of Season 1, Spider-Man and Doctor Strange team up to fight a mysterious symbiote alien, who leaves behind a small trace of symbiotic goo that Osborn collects and investigates. It’s revealed that one of Doctor Strange’s time-traveling portals accidentally sent the spider that bit Peter back in time, and that’s how he got his superpowers in the first place. It’s also revealed that Richard Parker, Peter’s father who was presumed dead, is in fact alive and imprisoned when Aunt May goes to visit him. 


	The cast includes Grace Song as Nico Minoru, Kari Wahlgren as Aunt May, Eugene Byrd as Lonnie Lincoln/Tombstone, Zeno Robinson as Harry Osborn, Hugh Dancy as Otto Octavius/Doctor Octopus, Charlie Cox as Daredevil.

schema.headline: ‘Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man’ Season 2 Sets Release Date

title: Marvel’s ‘Zodiac’ Sets 2028 Release on Disney+ as New Details Revealed
description:
Marvel Television revealed the first logo for its new series “Zodiac,” a live-action spy thriller set for release in 2028.

	The series will begin s
body:
Marvel Television revealed the first logo for its new series “Zodiac,” a live-action spy thriller set for release in 2028.

	The series will begin shooting in London in the spring, Marvel Television chief Brad Winderbaum said during its New York Comic-Con panel, with casting beginning in the “next couple of weeks.”

	No additional details were immediately available.


	“Zodiac” marks the first new live-action show that’s been announced for Marvel since last year’s “Ironheart.” While the MCU had a massive hit on the big-screen with “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” breaking records at the box office, the TV universe had some popular shows come to an end.
	

	Just a few months after it premiered in January, “Wonder Man” was canceled — despite being renewed for a second season and landing an Emmy nomination for lead actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. The show was critically acclaimed, and it made Abdul-Mateen II the first live-action actor to receive an Emmy nod for both a Marvel and DC series after he starred in HBO’s “Watchmen.”

	Then, it was revealed that “Daredevil: Born Again” would end with next year’s Season 3. The series revived Charlie Cox’s popular street-level hero after he debuted in Netflix’s “Daredevil” show. Season 3 looks to be a long-awaited reunion for the Netflix “Defenders” heroes, including Krysten Ritter as Jessica Jones, Mike Colter as Luke Cage and Finn Jones as Iron First.

	“VisionQuest” is set to premiere on Oct. 14 and will cap off the trilogy of shows that began with “WandaVision” and then “Agatha All Along.” After starring in “WandaVision,” Paul Bettany is back as the robot Vision, who’s been hiding out and communicating with other AI androids brought to life, like Ultron, J.A.R.V.I.S., F.R.I.D.A.Y. and more.

schema.headline: Marvel’s ‘Zodiac’ Sets 2028 Release on Disney+ as New Details Revealed

title: Colin Jost, Danny Chun Set New Comedy Series ‘6 Bed 1 Bath,’ Produced Outside Studio System
description:
Colin Jost and “The Office” writer Danny Chun are launching a new, original comedy series produced outside the Hollywood studio system.

	Titled “6
body:
Colin Jost and “The Office” writer Danny Chun are launching a new, original comedy series produced outside the Hollywood studio system.

	Titled “6 Bed 1 Bath,” the sitcom follows a group of five roommates in their 20s who share an apartment with a man who has lived there since 1982 and continued to build new bedrooms every time his rent increased, per the logline. The series recently wrapped production in New York City and will premiere across free, ad-supported video-on-demand platforms, such as Tubi, Pluto TV and the Roku Channel.
	

	“6 Bed 1 Bath” was not produced by a major studio or streamer. Instead, Jost and Chun, who first worked together at the Harvard Lampoon, teamed up with the independent Revue Studios, which financed and structured the project around brand partnerships. The partnerships — facilitated by Revue, CAA Entertainment Partnerships and production companies These Pictures and No Notes — allowed Jost and Chun to retain full creative control of the series.


	“Danny and I just wanted to make a show we thought was funny and somehow those are the hardest shows to get made,” said Jost. “So we found a new, innovative way to do it outside of the normal studio system and we feel very lucky about how the cast and the crew came together. We’re excited for everyone to see it.”

	Three-time Emmy winner Jost joined “Saturday Night Live” in 2005 and currently serves as the co-anchor of “Weekend Update” with Michael Che. Chun began his career writing for “The Simpsons” before he joined “The Office.” He is currently executive producing a film he wrote for Sony Animation and has feature projects set up at both Sony and Dreamworks Animation.
	

	“6 Bed 1 Bath” is executive produced by Jost, Scarlett Johansson, Chun, Andrew Singer, Jeff Grosvenor, Jonathan Lia, Ryan Case, Molly McMillen and Jon Liebman.

title: VIFF, Málaga Film Festival Launch Emerging Filmmaker Exchange
description: The Vancouver International Film Festival’s Institute for the Moving Image has announced a new partnership with Spain’s Málaga Film Festival to laun
body:
The Vancouver International Film Festival’s Institute for the Moving Image has announced a new partnership with Spain’s Málaga Film Festival to launch an exchange between their respective emerging-talent programs – the Málaga Talent program and VIFF Catalyst.

	The first filmmaker selected from this year’s Catalyst participants is Diego Minor Martínez, a Mexico-born filmmaker who is now based in Vancouver. The Málaga Talent’s program is aimed at filmmakers under 30 and is conducted in Spanish. Martínez will travel to Spain to participate early next year, while a participant from Málaga Talent’s 2027 cohort will come to Vancouver for Catalyst later that year. There’s no age limit for Catalyst.
	

	The exchange gives filmmakers not just access to new markets and potential collaborators, but is also designed to give them exposure to a different culture and industry at an early stage of their careers, when international relationships can potentially shape future projects.


	“This is a way to bring a new experience to that specific participant, connecting with a market that maybe will be interesting to explore,” Ana Belén Asfura, director of the Institute for the Moving Image, tells Variety.

	Asfura, who attended Málaga this year as part of Mafiz, the festival’s industry program, says the relationship grew out of conversations with the team there, including with Mafiz director Annabelle Aramburu. “Hopefully this partnership will open other things that we are also discussing with Málaga, in terms of bringing a delegation of producers and companies from Spain next year as well.”
	

	The exchange removes some of the financial barriers for emerging filmmakers that would otherwise make international opportunities inaccessible — covering flights, accommodation and meals.

	The Catalyst program includes 10 sessions, roughly three hours each, covering areas including production, grants, distribution, marketing and post-production. Participants also get to visit local studios and receive access to all of VIFF’s programming including industry events, panels, masterclasses, the AMP Music Media Summit and film screenings.

	Asfura sees international collaboration as increasingly important not only as a financing strategy, but because audiences themselves have become more global and culturally diverse.

	“If you think about every country, we have a multicultural background everywhere,” she says. “We need to try to attend to those needs of the audience.”

	Building new partnerships and relationships around the world, ultimately, helps fulfill the needs of the audience, she argues.

	“I think that’s more of a globalized vision that we have. And we understand that growth as a creator is about that. It’s about knowing other cultures, knowing other ways to tell stories.”

	There’s a difference in how various countries and cultures tell stories, and through exchanges like this, filmmakers have an opportunity to pick up new approaches.

	This is the first partnership with an international film festival, but Asfura hopes this is only the first step toward bringing in more in the years to follow.

	“We have a great group of Indigenous content creators here, and I think it would be super beneficial for them, for example, to take part in other programs that are focused on Indigenous communities in other places — for example, in Norway or in Brazil.”

	It’s important for her to see filmmakers get these opportunities at an early stage, because, she says, “you have more space to grow.”

schema.headline: VIFF, Málaga Film Festival Launch Emerging Filmmaker Exchange

title: Hugh Jackman on His Morning Routine, Meditation and Starring in Ridley Scott’s ‘Treasure Island’: ‘This Script Was Just Undeniable’
description: Hugh Jackman takes his morning routine seriously. The actor, who has spent decades maintaining the stamina required to play Wolverine and perform ei
body:
Hugh Jackman takes his morning routine seriously. The actor, who has spent decades maintaining the stamina required to play Wolverine and perform eight shows a week on Broadway, is an early riser, a devoted meditator and, apparently, not above breaking into song during a workout.

	It’s a fitting premise for his latest campaign with AG1, the daily nutritional supplement brand that named Jackman its global ambassador earlier this year. In a new spot, the actor puts his musical theater chops to work, singing his way through a workout while touting the benefits of his daily greens. The partnership is more than a celebrity endorsement: Jackman has been using AG1 for more than five years, after it was recommended by his doctor, and has been a strategic investor in the company since 2021.


	“I get offered a lot of things, and I just figured it’s got to be something that makes sense to me, that I really believe in, and that I actually use,” he says.



	Below, Jackman talks to Variety about his daily wellness rituals, 30-year meditation practice, his upcoming role in Ridley Scott’s “Treasure Island” and, yes, Wolverine’s future in the MCU.
	
		What does your morning routine look like — and what’s the first thing that tends to fall apart when you’re in the middle of a film shoot?	

	If I’m getting up very early, I will not meditate straight away when I get up. But I’ve been a meditator for 30 years. Sometimes I’ll wait, do it at lunchtime, but I’ve kind of learned my lesson. No matter what the call time is for filming, I still just get up a little bit earlier and get everything done.


	It’s better. I mean, there’s not much difference between waking up at four a.m. and waking up at six. It’s kind of the same, ultimately.
	
		So you’re one of those people that can survive off of not that much sleep?	

	Well, I still like seven, eight hours. Sometimes more if I can. But I was not a morning person until I had a job opening up a gym, which I opened up at six a.m. I slept in twice, and I basically was told, “You do not want to be late for the people who are turning up for that six a.m. workout.” No matter how nice you are, they will not give you too many tries. So then I used to set three alarms, and that sort of changed it. Really, from that moment on, I was a morning person.
	
		How does your location affect your routine and lifestyle?	

	One of my favorite things, if I’m in Australia — I live right on the beach — I will always get up before the sun gets up because I can be in the water as the sun comes up. And I just think, ‘Why isn’t everyone on the planet doing this?’ You never feel better.

	I do way more walking in New York than anywhere else. Even though it’s probably the most condensed city, I just walk everywhere, or I ride a bike everywhere. But I like to be active in the morning.
	
		You’ve worked with AG1 for a long time and you clearly love it. What did you actually notice when you started taking it that made you stick with it for so long?	

	That I wasn’t getting sick. For me, getting a cold, particularly as I sing and I do concerts or being on stage, it’s got a little more weight to it.

	If you get a cold, you go into the office, or even if you’re doing a play, you’re like, “Oh, sniffle.” But when you’re singing, it’s really important. My doctor just said, “Man, you’re a busy guy. It’s hard to get everything you need. It’s almost impossible to get everything you need just through nutrition with a busy lifestyle. Take this, and then you’re covered foundationally, like your gut health.” And so I just noticed that I was waking up a little faster, I was not getting sick, and I just felt better.


						
			
	

	
					
	
		In the campaign video, you start singing during your workout. I know musicians sometimes run on the treadmill while they’re singing their sets to rehearse. Do you ever do that?	

	Absolutely. Particularly if you’re going to tap dance, or you’re dancing, or if you’re doing something like that, any song-and-dance number. I notice it’s the fittest I will ever be because singing — it’s one thing to just run fast and be out of breath and your heart rate’s going 170, but to be able to hold your breath, if you think about it, you’re singing a long phrase. You don’t want to be taking a breath every three seconds while you’re singing. So you have to be calm and still have lung capacity whilst your heart rate’s going 160. And every time I finish a show and I go for a run, I can run forever. So you have to practice singing whilst running, jumping rope or doing whatever.

	
		I feel like Taylor Swift was the first person I saw doing that routine, and then I realized this is just a completely normal routine for singers.	

	The first person I heard about doing it, I remember when I was young, was Mick Jagger. He went on that world tour and he said, “In order to do what I do, I have to be running 10, 15 miles a day.” And when you’re traveling, being fit is key for sleep. I think sleep is the number one factor for me.
	
		You did say you were going to play Wolverine until you were in your 90s, so—	

	To be clear, Ryan Reynolds said that. 
	
		Meditation is another one of your non-negotiables. How did you get into meditation?	

	I learned meditation originally through the School of Practical Philosophy, which I was introduced to by a friend when I was doing acting. You know when you’re around people and you feel they’ve got something about them, you can’t put your finger on it? I literally said that to him. I said, “There’s something about you, man.” His name was Warwick. I said, “Warwick, there’s something about you. I don’t know what it is, but I kind of feel like I want it, whatever that is.” And he goes, “Oh, I started meditating.” I’m like, “What? What is that?” And he goes, “It’s transcendental meditation” and it changed everything. And it did.

	I was 22, 23, and it really changed everything. It gives me a place to, what I call, kind of coming home to myself twice a day, no matter what’s going on. So the surface of the water, which is our life — right now, for you and I, it’s pretty calm on the surface — but whatever’s happening on the surface, if you sink down to the bottom of the ocean, it’s always calm and peaceful. And that is what meditation represents to me. So it’s like a twice-a-day reminder of what is there under the surface.A
	
		You’re set to star in Ridley Scott’s “Treasure Island.” How did Ridley sell you on this character that people already know so well?	

	Really, it was the script. I know Ridley and Ridley goes, “Dude.” He sent me the script, and I just read it. I had never read the book, had never seen the movie. I knew various things about it. I actually didn’t know how foundational it was — the idea of a treasure map, the pirate and the parrot and all. I was like, “Oh, they came from that.” And Jack Thorne, who famously wrote “Adolescence” and did “Harry Potter” for the stage show — this script was just undeniable. I was just like, “Oh, this is amazing.” That was it.

	
		What was it about his take on the material that surprised you?	

	All I knew was I had no idea where it was going, and I was very surprised but satisfied at the end.
	
		You’ve said you’re not going to be in “Doomsday” — but are you going to be in “Secret Wars”?	

	I don’t know what you’re talking about. I have no idea what you’re talking about.
	
		I had to ask, but that was a very civilized answer.	

	I do have an internal chip, that is not metaphorical. There’s a literal chip, and if I say the wrong thing, I get shut down. I don’t know who controls that chip, but someone is controlling it.

schema.headline: Hugh Jackman on His Morning Routine, Meditation and Starring in Ridley Scott’s ‘Treasure Island’: ‘This Script Was Just Undeniable’

title: ‘Carrie’ Finale Burning Question: Who Is Adelaide? Kate Siegel on Why Her Mysterious Character ‘Controls This Story’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains major spoilers from the 2026 series “Carrie,” now streaming on Prime Video.

	Kate Siegel knows how to speak Step
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains major spoilers from the 2026 series “Carrie,” now streaming on Prime Video.

	Kate Siegel knows how to speak Stephen King. She was reading his work long before she probably should have, and has often retreated to it in times of need.

	“He was my dad’s favorite author, and when he passed away, I must have read ‘The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon’ 50 times just to get through the grief,” Siegel tells Variety.

	Her familiarity with King’s vast writings also meant she knew exactly which of his characters to draw upon when asked to play something completely new within his sandbox. Prime Video’s new version of “Carrie” isn’t the first adaptation of King’s classic tale of a childhood gone wrong, nor is it Siegel’s first time working with series creator Mike Flanagan. She’s married to the fellow King whisperer, and previously starred in Flanagan’s film adaptations of “Gerald’s Game” and “The Life of Chuck” –– not to mention all of his original Netflix series.



	

					Summer H. Howell
									Courtesy of Prime Video
	




	But when it comes to “Carrie,” she isn’t playing a single King creation, per se. Anyone familiar with the “Carrie” story knows exactly where the new series ends up after eight episodes. A reluctantly reclusive and telepathically gifted Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) tries to assimilate into high school, only to be ridiculed and manipulated by the savagery of her peers. When she thinks she has finally won them over by being crowned prom queen, she’s doused in pig’s blood and unleashes fiery hell on her town. Nearly all the show’s storylines and characters are pulled directly from King’s text.

	But among the exceptions is Siegel’s character, who is only heard as the narrator throughout the first seven episodes before making her onscreen debut in the finale.


	The character’s name is Adelaide, seemingly the headmistress of a home for gifted young women and the person behind the camera of the talking head interviews that have teased the terror to come all season. She’s interviewing the survivors of the prom night massacre, in search of the elusive culprit behind the carnage, Carrie, and her astral projecting enabler, Emaline (Thalia Dudek).


	“It was an honor to step into this idea of a character that I’ve seen hints of in different stories [from King],” Siegel says. “There’s a woman like this in ‘The Institute.’ There are women like this in ‘Carrie,’ the original novel. There are some women like this in ‘Firestarter.’ But we don’t know which way Adelaide’s going to go. We don’t know whose side Adelaide is on. We don’t know a lot about her, but I’m familiar enough with the type of women that Stephen King likes to write that I could sort of hum the melody of who she is.”
	



	

									Courtesy of Prime Video
	



	Siegel and Flanagan spent plenty of time discussing the character, but he initially held back anything that might reveal who he wants her to become should the series continue.

	“One of his favorite answers when I would ask about her past or her future or who she is, would just be, ‘Yeah, it’s crazy, right? Great question,’” she says. “And then he’d just move on!”
	

	Siegel has since been clued in on Adelaide’s potential, and she’s gotten quite skilled at the art of the dodge as the series leaves viewers with few answers. “The questions people should be asking are, why is Adelaide filming these interviews and who is she telling this story to?” Siegel says, teasingly. “Of course she is interested in Carrie and wants to know everything about her, but to what end? We don’t want to give away too much, even though right now it’s only Season 1 — and we don’t know if anything else will happen.”

	The other major clue viewers get about Adelaide is that she is also gifted, and she’s not afraid to wield those gifts as she sees fit. In the final moments of the season, she interviews Margaret White (Samantha Sloyan), Carrie’s religious mother who, in this version, survives her daughter’s prom night wrath thanks to her own repressed telekinetic abilities. But when Margaret refuses to even consider exploring these newly rekindled gifts further, Adelaide deems her unworthy of this unexpected second chance. Using telepathy, she instructs Maragret’s mind to slowly stop her own heartbeat, ultimately killing her. It’s a calculated act that lets Adelaide flex her own powers.



	

					Samantha Sloyan
									Courtesy of Robert Falconer/Prime Video
	



	Siegel says that scene is key, not just because of what Adelaide does, but how she does it –– or rather, says it. Siegel narrates the cold opens of each episode, but she was very mindful of Adelaide’s onscreen voice, which is measured and changes its cadence when she goes from interviewing Maragret to killing her. She found inspiration for that voice in an unexpected place.

	“You know the show ‘Couples Therapy’ on Showtime?” Siegel says. “The therapist who runs that program, Dr. Orna [Guralnik], has a very neutral kind of questioning tone until she gets to something that she’d like to dig a little deeper on. She’s also always touching her face while she’s listening. I just love the way she does it. That was the beginning of putting on Adelaide, as if it was just gently suggesting that we go a little deeper.”

	One such instance is when Adelaide casually drops the word that will send King fans into a frenzy. Speaking to Margaret, she says, “A lot of people have a little bit of shine and don’t even know it.” That, of course, is a reference to the psychic abilities featured in “The Shining” and other King books. But the word “shine” isn’t in the original “Carrie” novel.

	“I was so happy that we were allowed to have that word, because Adelaide sits there on a throne of chaotic neutral,” Siegel says. “She doesn’t care if you’re good or bad. She’s really looking for this one thing, and she believes every woman could have it. She’s waiting, and she’s thinking, and she’s seeing. And then she says that word. I think Adelaide’s voice has a lot of power, so she’s very careful with it.”

	While the series has not yet been renewed for Season 2, if this is all “Carrie” gets, it has been a family affair for the entire Siegel/Flanagan household. In addition to Siegel’s debut in the finale, the episode also features their daughter Theo as a young Margaret, during a flashback to the first time she conjures her gifts. Episode 3 also marks the first time Siegel has directed an episode of television (she previously made her directorial debut on a segment of “V/H/S/Beyond”).
	

	Her episode, titled “Social Studies,” is among the season’s most important, as it depicts Carrie’s first high school party, a rite of passage that has ripple effects all the way to the finale. But due to the production schedule, it actually shot after her onscreen debut as Adelaide. Episodes 1, 2, 7 and 8, all directed by Flanagan, were shot as a super block at the top of production. Then, Siegel was up next to direct Episode 3.

	To prepare, she plastered her workspace with photos of her and her friends at high school parties in the early 2000s for inspiration. It also gave her an excuse to revisit the classic ‘90s parties depicted in movies “Can’t Hardly Wait” and “10 Things I Hate About You.”



	

					Summer H. Howell, Joel Oulette
									Courtesy of Prime Video
	



	“It’s a very specific type of joy, because there’s anticipation, right?” Siegel says. “And nine times out of 10, a house party doesn’t quite deliver. But when a house party does deliver after the whole day of anticipation, and you’re a teenager and you’ve never really experienced this joy, it is so magical. That is what I wanted for Carrie.”

	Not only does Carrie dance with her classmates, but also has an intoxicated (and intoxicatingly) platonic bonding moment with Tommy (Joel Oulette), the dreamy boy who genuinely befriends her as they lay on the front lawn of the party and talk about the stars. When Tommy dies as collateral damage of Carrie’s violence in the finale, his final words will be about those same stars. Having seen the finale before she got behind the camera, Siegel was able to consciously stitch these moments together.

	After leaving the party, Tommy drives Carrie home and the bliss of experiencing a good night out after a life of captivity literally causes her to levitate his car off the road.

	“One of Amazon’s favorite moments in the script was that car lift, and same for me,” Siegel says. “There’s a beautiful dichotomy in Episode 3, where with Carrie’s confusion and frustration and concern, she can lift a raindrop. But with her joy, she can float a car. It has a built-in melancholy, because we all know how this story ends. We know it ends in the death of Tommy. We know it ends in carnage, and it makes it even worse to see them that happy and that joyful.”
	

	One of Siegel’s proudest directorial decisions was this scene’s other half. At the same party, Chris (Alison Thornton), the chief designer of Carrie’s torment, has the worst party of her life. As Carrie hangs her head out Tommy’s window to take in every last euphoric second of the night, a blacked-out Chris stares blankly into the future.

	“That back-and-forth shot between them was not in the original script,” she says. “That was something I pitched to Mike. The weight of Chris’ grief and sadness about her parents’ divorce and being replaced, and all these concerns about who she is and who she will be, cut with the lightness of Carrie feeling like she found her people. We really need that as we move forward in the story, and see these two butt heads.”

	Because she played Adelaide first and then went behind the camera, Siegel held a great deal of power in guiding the viewer from the best night of Carrie’s life to the worst. In a way, she shares that bit of control with her character, whoever she is.

	“Adelaide is the narrator of this story,” she says. “And the reason I like that is because it means one thing for the first seven episodes. But once you realize what she’s doing in the eighth, you see she’s been molding and framing this story. Adelaide controls this story — and never let it be said that Kate Siegel doesn’t love control.”

schema.headline: ‘Carrie’ Finale Burning Question: Who Is Adelaide? Kate Siegel on Why Her Mysterious Character ‘Controls This Story’

title: Rodrigo Santoro and Camila Pitanga to Star in Marcelo Gomes’ ‘Garota da Urca’ From a Script by Luciana Paes and Leonardo Moreira (EXCLUSIVE)
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Two of Brazil’s biggest screen stars, Rodrigo Santoro (“The Blue Trail”) and Camila Pitanga (“Basic Sanitation, the Movie”)
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Two of Brazil’s biggest screen stars, Rodrigo Santoro (“The Blue Trail”) and Camila Pitanga (“Basic Sanitation, the Movie”), are set to star in “Garota da Urca” (“Girl From Urca”), the new film by renowned director Marcelo Gomes. “Oxygen Masks Will Not Drop Automatically” writer Leonardo Moreira and veteran writer-actor Luciana Paes are now confirmed to write the script. “Garota da Urca” is a co-production between Matizar Filmes and Misti Filmes.
	

	Gomes and Santoro sat down with Variety after a lengthy conversation at the Rio Film Festival, where they expressed their mutual admiration and discussed their decades in film. Santoro, who recently starred in Gabriel Mascaro’s Berlin-winning “The Blue Trail,” is one of Brazil’s most successful screen exports, having starred in major Hollywood productions such as Richard Curtis’s “Love Actually” and Zack Snyder’s “300.” Gomes broke out into the international scene with “Cinema, Aspirins and Vultures,” which screened at Cannes’s Un Certain Regard in 2005, and has since directed major films such as “I Travel Because I Have to, I Come Back Because I Love You,” “Joaquim,” and “Paloma.”


	As for Pitanga, the actress is one of Brazil’s most popular telenovela stars, as well as having starred in films such as “I’d Receive the Worst News from Your Beautiful Lips” and “Basic Sanitation, The Movie,” which saw her share the screen with Oscar nominees Fernanda Torres (“I’m Still Here”) and Wagner Moura (“The Secret Agent”). 
	

	Gomes prefers to keep the finer details of “Garota da Urca” under wraps, but says it is about a married couple approaching their 50s and dealing with the existential questions that come with middle age. Gomes proves ahead of the curve in his desire to tell an adult comedy about sex and love, working on his latest at a time when films like Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite” are proving greatly successful with audiences. “We’ve been working on this project for over three years, so this has been a very happy coincidence,” he says of the momentum.



	

					‘Oxygen Masks Will (Not) Drop Automatically’
									Courtesy of HBO/Max
	



	“Cinema, as Tarkovsky once said, is space and time,” he adds. “This is precisely what I want to broach with the film: the space of Rio de Janeiro beyond Ipanema, and time, with people in constant dialogue about the effects of the passage of time, of how time affects the maturing of feelings.”

	The director adds that “Garota da Urca” is about “understanding how we can preserve those emotions from a first date as time goes on.” “It’s not about whether or not love resists the passage of time; it’s about facing how we change over time,” he goes on. “This is the idea of the film, and we wanted to invite actors who were at the same point in life as the characters and able to lend some of this existential crisis to the people they’ll play on screen. That’s how we got to Camila and Rodrigo, and I am thrilled to be undergoing this journey with such talented actors.”

	Santoro echoes this feeling of admiration, saying he has been a fan of the director for over 20 years and an admirer of how Gomes is a “filmmaker who loves his characters.”

	“I feel very grateful for the opportunity to make this film with him because I can already imagine the process of making the film, which, to me, is the most precious thing,” he adds.

	“I don’t pay much mind to the taboos around turning 50, but I acknowledge they exist,” continues the actor. “There is this social construct and mythology around 50, but there is also something that happens within us: you have lived a long life and acquired great experience while, at the same time, there is still so much ahead and you still feel such energy for living. I think it’s a very interesting moment of life, but I want to make known I am not facing a crisis in my marriage [laughs]. I have a wonderful marriage, two beautiful, healthy daughters, and all is well.”
	

	“Still, I am a man, an actor, who is in my early 50s and questioning things related to being a 50-year-old man in the world of today,” he notes. “I always say the work of an actor is very therapeutic, because I end up examining my own questions through my characters. This character will deal with the obscure, and it’s an opportunity I find very precious. I feel very intrigued.”

	Seeing Santoro and Pitanga share the screen is also a highly enticing prospect to Brazilian audiences, who last saw the duo together in the immensely popular 2004 telenovela “Mulheres Apaixonadas.”

	“This thing with Camila is curious because we had a moment during the novela despite not being a couple,” says Santoro. “That moment did so well with audiences; the characters were so well-received, and now, with the digital phenomenon of our era, social media has resurrected that novela and one of our scenes together. I thought it was curious, but also great timing, when Marcelo told me he had both of us in mind. I’m very much looking forward to working together.”

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					“You Can See Everything”
	




	2027 Academy Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Oct. 8, 2026): Lots of moving pieces as the season treads along.

	The New York Film Festival gave the first set of eyes on Luca Guadagnino’s intense dramedy “Artificial,” which could be a major player for Neon, who picked it up after Amazon MGM Studios dumped it earlier in the year. The film could be a force in multiple categories including best picture and supporting actor for Andrew Garfield, who could be the big spoiler if the season breaks his way.

	NYFF is about to conclude with Ava DuVernay’s documentary feature “14th,” which will have a new original song by Brittany Howard and Robert Glasper.

	Other buzzy movies include Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything,” which screened at NYFF and in Los Angeles, where it received a rapturous response. As the days continue, it’s looking like we could have our very first nonfiction movie nominated for best picture. Whether or not it makes the ultimate documentary feature shortlist will continue to plague pundits.

	Entries for the Golden Globes continue to break around the industry. Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care” will enter the comedy categories, along with Curry Barker’s “Obsession,” which has some on social media scratching their heads.

	This week’s updates are below.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

            A wrestler in Mexico was arrested and hit with criminal charges after he slammed a referee to the canvas during a match and apparently killed him ... and it's all on video.
      
    
            Shocking footage shows Hijo de Fishman -- a wrestler clad in a facemask and green pants -- picking up legendary ref Gerardo Germán Pineda and slamming him to the ground. The ref rolls around on the canvas, seemingly in pain.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            According to reports ... Hijo de Fishman later performed a piledriver on Pineda, who fell unconscious after the move and was ultimately pronounced dead at the venue.
      

            Hijo de Fishman was detained and later handed over to prosecutors on a culpable homicide charge ... akin to manslaughter.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Steph Heredia, an onlooker quoted in The Daily Star, claimed the wrestler argued with the official before executing the move. She says she and other members of the crowd thought the piledriver was just part of the show.
      
    
            Pineda -- a former wrestler-turned-referee known as El Búho -- worked in wrestling for decades. He was 75 years old.
